 A Fruit Buffet for Monkeys Still Happens Here. Lately, Many Guests Eat in a Cage.
 Home › Travel Insights › Food & Culture A Fruit Buffet for Monkeys Still Happens Here. Lately, Many Guests Eat in a Cage.
 Lopburi, Thailand, has fed its macaques a November banquet since 1989. As they multiplied, many were moved into enclosures, and the feast followed.
 By Rolando Herrera Last Updated Nov 15, 2026 7 min read Share Native Email Whatsapp Facebook X Linkedin Macaques eat scattered fruit near Phra Prang Sam Yot in Lopburi in 2017. Adam Jones from Kelowna, BC, Canada · Monkeys at Prang Sam Yot (Monkey Temple) – Lop Buri – Thailand – 05 (35028507555).jpg · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Cropped and resized from a Commons 1920-pixel rendition In This Article A Hotelier’s Thank-You When the Guests Took Over What the Feast Looks Like Now The Temple Behind the Tables Going on November 29 Where In The World Lopburi; approximate world location Thailand Lopburi Overview · Natural Earth In This Article 
 Jump To A Section A Hotelier’s Thank-You When the Guests Took Over What the Feast Looks Like Now The Temple Behind the Tables Going on November 29 Share Native Email Whatsapp Facebook X Linkedin In November 1989, a hotel owner in Lopburi, a town about 150 kilometers north of Bangkok, set out banquet tables for some unusual guests. Yongyuth Kitwatananusont, who ran the Lopburi Inn, laid fruit, vegetables and sweets in front of the town’s 13th-century Khmer temple, Phra Prang Sam Yot, and let the long-tailed macaques that lived there eat their fill. He wanted to thank the monkeys for the visitors they drew and for the luck he believed they brought his business.
 The Monkey Buffet Festival became one of Thailand’s best-known oddities. For decades, photographers waited at the ruins while monkeys swarmed tables piled with watermelon, bananas and sticky rice. Then the monkeys outgrew the town. Since 2024, Lopburi has been moving its macaques into enclosures, and at the 2024 festival many of the buffet’s guests ate their feast behind bars. EPA photographs from November 24, 2024, show captured monkeys eating fruit, vegetables and desserts inside an enclosure.

 The Feast Monkey Buffet Festival Usually Last Sunday of Nov. Since 1989 
 A Hotelier’s Thank-You 
 The first banquet was modest. Vice reported that Yongyuth started it in 1989 as a small celebration of his company’s success, and a local tourism history describes the first event as 35 Chinese-style banquet tables at three spots in town. Over the following decades it grew into a staged spectacle with an opening ceremony, dancers in monkey costumes and tables built into towers of fruit, with support from the Tourism Authority of Thailand.
 The quantities grew too. In a Reuters interview from an earlier festival, Yongyuth said he had spent 400,000 baht on food, about two tons of fruit and nearly a ton of vegetables. Vice reported a later year with more than 100 tables and about 2,000 kilograms of fruit and vegetables. Yongyuth told Vice that when he began, there were about 300 monkeys in town. By the time of that interview, he estimated about 4,000.
 The idea draws on local belief. Lopburi’s macaques have long been linked with Hanuman, the monkey hero of the Ramakien, Thailand’s version of the Ramayana, and the animals living around the ruins and the nearby San Phra Kan shrine were treated as lucky residents. Feeding them, in this view, repays a debt.
 Macaques at Phra Prang Sam Yot in Lopburi in 2017. Adam Jones from Kelowna, BC, Canada · Monkeys at Prang Sam Yot (Monkey Temple) – Lop Buri – Thailand – 04 (34896511431).jpg · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Cropped and resized from a Commons 1920-pixel rendition 
 Yongyuth also turned himself into part of the show. Reporting for The World , Patrick Winn described a host who tried to outdo himself each year, at one point arriving by parachute in a monkey suit. Winn counted more than 3,000 macaques living in the town and a feast that promised 4,000 kilograms of food that year, more than the year before. He also noted that, although Buddhism long ago replaced Hinduism as the majority religion, many Buddhists in Lopburi see caring for the monkeys as a way of making merit.
 The festival did what it was designed to do. Lopburi, a provincial town with a handful of ruins, became a name international travelers recognized. The World described the event’s real purpose plainly as attracting tourists, and the photographs it produced every November reached newspapers around the world. For years the monkeys around the temple were themselves the attraction, posing on the towers and climbing on visitors for treats.
 When the Guests Took Over 
 The feeding helped create a problem. With easy food from tourists and residents, the macaque population rose sharply. The animals raided shops and homes, snatched phones and food, bit people and fought in gangs in the old town. By 2024 Lopburi’s mayor, Jamroen Salacheep, told The Nation that the city had become almost a ghost town.
 The city and Thailand’s Department of National Parks responded with sterilization and capture. The Nation reported that the plan called for macaques to be moved into a shelter of more than 13 rai, about 2 hectares, in the Pho Kao Ton area of Lopburi’s Muang district. Thai PBS reported that some aggressive monkeys were relocated to a shelter in Nakhon Nayok province. By late 2024, Reuters footage showed caged monkeys being offered the annual banquet.
 The enclosures have not ended the trouble. Khaosod English reported in November 2024 that about 200 monkeys escaped from an enclosure and some got into a police station, and UPI reported another escape in June 2026. In February 2026 the city appealed for funds to keep managing the animals. Lopburi still has monkeys around its ruins, but far fewer roam the streets than before.
 What the Feast Looks Like Now 
 The festival still runs on the last Sunday of November. Planning guides expect the 2026 edition on Sunday, November 29, though the program is set each year by local organizers and the Tourism Authority of Thailand’s Lopburi office. A traveler guide updated in October 2026, Visit Thailand Today , describes the main banquet now taking place at the monkey shelter, with smaller events still possible at Phra Prang Sam Yot.
 That changes what you see. The classic photographs show monkeys climbing over tables in front of the three towers of the Khmer temple. Inside the shelter, the animals eat in large cages, which welfare campaigners have criticized. The opening ceremony, with music and dance, and the street food that springs up around the festival still make it a lively day in town.
 The playfulness starts before the day. A 2026 feature by Seasia described locals handing out paper invitations tied to cashews in the days before the festival, as if the macaques were guests who needed a formal card. On the day, the opening ceremony features performers dressed as monkeys before the food is unveiled.
 The food is meant to be monkey-friendly but generous. Past menus have included watermelon, bananas, pineapples, corn, sticky rice and desserts, sometimes frozen into blocks of ice so the monkeys have to work for it. In earlier years, organizers ran several sittings through the day, at about 10 a.m., noon, 2 p.m. and 4 p.m., so photographers and families could each find a turn.
 Phra Prang Sam Yot, Lopburi’s 13th-century Khmer temple, in January 2024. Dominic Nelson · Lopburi – Phra Prang Sam Yot view from road.jpg · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Cropped and resized from a Commons 1920-pixel rendition 
 The relocation has changed daily life in the old town. Streets that monkeys once ruled are quieter, and the festival that celebrated them now has fewer monkeys roaming the ruins. Wildlife officials have also had to manage four kinds of macaque in the province, including the common long-tailed and rhesus macaques and the rarer pig-tailed and stump-tailed species, according to reporting from The Nation relayed by The Thaiger .
 The Temple Behind the Tables 
 Phra Prang Sam Yot is worth seeing with or without monkeys. The three linked towers were built in the Khmer style in the 13th century, originally as a Hindu shrine to Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva, and were later adapted for Buddhism. They stand in the old town beside the railway line and are the symbol of Lopburi.
 The temple charges foreigners a small entry fee, about 50 baht in recent years, while the shrine of San Phra Kan across the tracks is free. Nearby, the Phra Narai Ratchaniwet palace complex, now the Somdet Phra Narai National Museum, is one of the better-preserved royal compounds from the Ayutthaya era and makes the town a good half-day even outside festival season.
 The monkeys that remain at the ruins are habituated to people, and they still grab. Take off sunglasses and hats, keep bags zipped and do not carry food in plastic bags. Do not feed them outside designated areas, and do not stare at or crouch near a monkey, which it can read as a challenge.
 Going on November 29 
 Lopburi is an easy day trip. Trains from Bangkok take about two hours, and vans and buses run as well. Many visitors combine it with Ayutthaya, which has more hotels and sits on the same rail line. Confirm the 2026 program with the Tourism Authority of Thailand before you go, since the venue and times have changed with the monkey relocation.
 If you want to stay overnight, book early. Lopburi has only a modest number of hotels, most near the old town and the station, and festival weekend is its busiest. Bring cash for street food and small entry fees, wear shoes you can walk in on uneven ground around the ruins, and leave anything dangling, from earrings to lanyards, in your room.
 Plan the rest of the trip around the season. Late November is the start of Thailand’s cool, dry high season, and most travelers base themselves in Bangkok. Our list of things to do in Bangkok covers the city before or after a Lopburi day trip. If you are adding a stop in Japan, our story on Hakone’s black eggs covers another food ritual built around a place, and Kyoto’s miso fortune crackers sell near another shrine full of animal symbolism. For more food traditions tied to a single day, see Oaxaca’s Night of the Radishes .
 The cage is the part to remember. A buffet that began as a hotelier’s thank-you to a few hundred temple monkeys helped feed a population into the thousands, and the feast continues today partly inside the shelters built to contain them.
